A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same task-arithmetic fairness study. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and the retained methods, dataset statistics, and Figures 1–11 support reliable matching despite substantial expansion and reformatting.

before.justification: v1 reports original hate-speech experiments comparing FFT, LoRA, and task arithmetic, including coefficient sweeps and subgroup-vector injection analyses in Figures 1–11.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original Civil Comments toxicity and UTKFace age-classification results in Appendices F–G and Tables 2–5.

M1.justification: The core procedures remain subgroup fine-tuning, computing parameter-difference task vectors, merging with a uniform scalar, and injecting selected subgroup vectors into FFT. The explicit single-scalar formulation clarifies a choice already present in v1 Section 4.2; additional evaluated architectures do not establish a new algorithm.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates only Berkeley D-Lab hate-speech detection. v2 adds Civil Comments toxicity classification and UTKFace binary age classification, extending coverage to another text population and to face images. Civil Comments covers gender and race with DistilBERT and gender with Qwen; UTKFace covers both attributes.

E2.justification: The evaluated comparator methods remain full fine-tuning, also called SFT in the new tables, and LoRA. These are extended to additional benchmarks. FairLoRA, FairTune, and other newly cited fairness methods are not added as evaluated comparators.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce validation-based coefficient selection, worst-case fairness metrics, two-epoch DistilBERT/Qwen training, different data fractions, and ViT image preprocessing. Section 2 also newly claims fairness-aware validation tuning, but Section 4.2 and Figure 1 retain training-accuracy selection for Berkeley. An actual protocol change or rerun of the original experiments is therefore not established.

E4.justification: The existing coefficient sweeps, subgroup-vector injection analyses, heatmaps, and distribution comparisons retain the same results in Figures 2–11. The added benchmark tables expand coverage but do not report new component ablations, perturbation tests, or sensitivity analyses.

E5.justification: v2 adds 95% confidence intervals, a stratified bootstrap protocol with 2,000 group-by-label-preserving resamples, and prediction pooling across seeds. Table 5 also adds intervals for the retained LLaMA comparisons. Original three-seed standard errors remain; increased training-run counts are not established, and DistilBERT task-addition rows remain point estimates.

E6.justification: Figures 1–11 retain their results, while Tables 2–5 and Appendix G add substantial new findings. For example, DistilBERT gender task addition reports accuracy 0.9395, worst-DPD 0.0454, and worst-EOD 0.3358. UTKFace race task-addition accuracy is 0.7227–0.7384, below SFT's 0.8463–0.8599. These are new experimental settings, not improvements over v1 scores.

T1.justification: v1 contains task-arithmetic equations and standard fairness definitions but no comparable theoretical analysis. v2 adds Section 5.1 and Appendix C: assumptions A1–A5, a weighted-ERM lemma, a thresholding lemma, and DPD/EOD bounds with proofs. The new derivations include an inconsistent normalization of the reference model.

C1.justification: v2 adds theoretical grounding as an explicit contribution and extends its main empirical claims to three datasets and four model families across text and vision. It also expressly scopes its novelty and conclusions to group fairness in binary classification, while retaining the original fairness-through-scaling claim.

C2.justification: v2 newly explains the observed trade-offs through group-weighted ERM and task-vector norms, rather than primarily describing empirical subgroup variation. Its limitations now explicitly address weight access, proprietary models, the expressiveness of one shared coefficient, and untested intersectional settings, extending v1's general dataset-dependence caveats.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-access link and a reproducibility statement describing configurations and reproduction scripts. It also documents DistilBERT/Qwen learning rates, epochs, batch sizes, sampling fractions and early stopping, plus ViT preprocessing. The original LLaMA hardware, software, and training details are retained.

R1.justification: Section 3 and Appendix A substantially expand positioning against fairness-aware PEFT, multi-task fairness, fairness composition, and vision-language bias audits, including FairLoRA, FairBranch, and Dwork and Ilvento. The earlier task-arithmetic efficiency discussion is relocated, not removed; bibliographic corrections alone do not account for this judgment.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, results overview, and conclusion/limitations undergo extensive rewriting. Existing appendix material is reorganized, part of related work moves into an extended appendix, and reproducibility and LLM-use statements are added. Author ordering, affiliations, and conference-header text also change.

P2.justification: The paper changes from two-column formatting to a single-column ICLR layout, resizing and relocating retained figures and tables. Tables 2–4 are added, with Table 5 consolidating some results and adding LLaMA intervals. Captions are revised, including correcting Figure 3's gender/race description and clarifying the separate injections in Figure 4.

improvement.justification: Broader text/vision evaluations, uncertainty reporting, and code-access information address v1's narrow empirical support. However, the new central theory treats an affine objective as quadratic in Appendix C.2 and inconsistently normalizes its reference model in C.3. Tuning descriptions also conflict, and Table 4 does not support the broad accuracy-preservation claim. These substantial empirical benefits and newly introduced validity problems prevent a reliable judgment of the net quality change.
